claim: Arabidopsis plants were exposed to two different hyperosmotic conditions (25 mM and 75 mM NaCl) for over five generations.
source: To evaluate the extent to which stress-induced transgenerational adaptation occurs, we first exposed Arabidopsis plants (Arabidopsis thaliana accession Col-0) to two different hyperosmotic conditions for over five generations (P0 of G1-G5, Figure 1A) (see Materials and methods for details).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the experimental design where plants were exposed to hyperosmotic stress conditions over multiple generations.

claim: Plants were subjected to stress only during the vegetative phase and were transferred to normal soil before most flowers formed.
source: Plants were subjected to stress only during the vegetative phase and were transferred to normal soil before most flowers formed; thereby reducing the possibility of parental stress exerting a direct effect on gametes (see Materials and methods for details).
evidence: The manuscript describes the specific timing of stress application to minimize direct effects on gametes.

claim: Seeds derived from G1-G5 treated and control plants were grown for two additional generations (P1 and P2) without stress.
source: To uncouple parent and progeny environments, we grew seeds derived from G1-G5 treated and control plants for two additional generations (P1 and P2) without stress (Figure 1A).
evidence: The experimental design explicitly includes growing progeny in stress-free conditions.

claim: The progeny derived from the first generation of stressed plants (G1) did not display significant signs of adaptation.
source: Similar to non-treated plants, the progeny derived from the first generation of stressed plants (G1) did not display significant signs of adaptation.
evidence: The manuscript reports phenotypic observations from the experiments.

claim: The direct progeny (P1) of G2-G5 stressed plants displayed higher germination and survival rates, and more robust vegetative growth on high-salinity (150 mM) medium.
source: In contrast, the direct progeny (P1) of G2-G5 stressed plants displayed higher germination and survival rates, and more robust vegetative growth on high-salinity (150 mM) medium (Figure 1B–C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1), suggesting that hyperosmotic priming requires repetitive exposure to stress.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing enhanced stress tolerance in progeny, supported by figures showing survival rates.

claim: Hyperosmotic priming requires repetitive exposure to stress.
source: In contrast, the direct progeny (P1) of G2-G5 stressed plants displayed higher germination and survival rates, and more robust vegetative growth on high-salinity (150 mM) medium (Figure 1B–C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1), suggesting that hyperosmotic priming requires repetitive exposure to stress.
evidence: The manuscript infers from the data that repeated stress exposure is necessary for adaptation.

claim: Adaptation was already lost in the second-generation progeny (P2) of G2-G5 stressed plants.
source: Notably, adaptation was already lost in the second-generation progeny (P2) of G2-G5 stressed plants.
evidence: The manuscript reports phenotypic observations showing loss of adaptation.

claim: Two generations of a stress-free environment were sufficient to revert the stress-induced changes.
source: Thus, two generations of a stress-free environment were sufficient to revert the stress-induced changes (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing reversion of adaptive phenotypes after two stress-free generations.

claim: Recurrent hyperosmotic stress in plants induces intergenerational adaptation, but this response does not persist in the absence of stress.
source: Our data thus suggest that recurrent hyperosmotic stress in plants induces intergenerational adaptation, but that this response does not persist in the absence of stress.
evidence: The manuscript draws conclusions from the experimental data about the transient nature of stress adaptation.

claim: Immediate progeny of stressed nrpd1a, cmt3, and ros1/dml2/dml3 (rdd) plants did not show enhanced survival under hyperosmotic stress conditions.
source: In contrast to progeny of stressed wild-type plants, immediate progeny of stressed nrpd1a (Herr et al., 2005) cmt3 (Chan et al., 2006) and ros1/dml2/dml3 (rdd) (Penterman et al., 2007) plants did not show enhanced survival under hyperosmotic stress conditions (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data from mutant analysis.

claim: Transgenerational adaptation to hyperosmotic stress relies in part on the DNA methylation machinery.
source: These data imply that transgenerational adaptation to hyperosmotic stress relies in part on the DNA methylation machinery, although these phenotypic data do not reveal how extensive the epigenetic changes are.
evidence: The manuscript infers from mutant phenotype data that DNA methylation machinery is involved in stress adaptation.

claim: Whole-genome bisulfite sequencing was performed on duplicate samples of leaf tissue from 10 plants each from the G1, G3 and G5 generations for each treatment.
source: To ensure statistically robust results, we excluded inter-individual epigenetic variation that can arise over the course of several generations (Becker et al., 2011; Schmitz et al., 2011) by collecting duplicate samples of leaf tissue from 10 plants each from the G1, G3 and G5 generations for each treatment (control, 25 mM-, and 75 mM-NaCl) (Figure 1A).
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental methodology for DNA methylation analysis.

claim: On average 6,866 DMPs (40% CG, 15% CHG and 45% CHH) were detected per generation in all pairwise comparisons.
source: Single-site polymorphisms between any two samples were rare, with on average 6,866 DMPs (40% CG, 15% CHG and 45% CHH) detected per generation in all pairwise comparisons (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative results from bisulfite sequencing analysis.

claim: Principal component analysis (PCA) and complete linkage clustering of methylation frequencies grouped all stress-treated samples (P0), separating them from control, P1, and P2 samples.
source: Principal component analysis (PCA) and complete linkage clustering of methylation frequencies grouped all stress-treated samples (P0), separating them from control, P1, and P2 samples (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: The manuscript presents statistical analysis results showing clustering patterns.

claim: Hyperosmotic stress had a small but noticeable effect on single methylated cytosines, and this effect was largely transient.
source: This indicated that hyperosmotic stress had a small but noticeable effect on single methylated cytosines, and that this effect was largely transient.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the clustering results to characterize the nature of methylation changes.

claim: Three times more methylation gains than losses were observed in salt-treated P0 plants compared to the control.
source: Overall we observed three times more methylation gains than losses in salt-treated P0 plants compared to the control (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative analysis of methylation changes.

claim: Only a small fraction of the DNA methylation changes reported by Jiang et al. (2014) were consistently induced by hyperosmotic stress.
source: Because we found considerably fewer DMPs than recently reported for multi-generational hyperosmotic stress treatments (Jiang et al., 2014), we re-analysed the published data. We found that only a small fraction of the DNA methylation changes reported by Jiang et al. (2014) were consistently induced by hyperosmotic stress (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The manuscript presents reanalysis of published data to compare with their findings.

claim: On average 24,700 methylated regions (MRs) per sample with a median length of 272 bp (mean: 856 bp) were identified.
source: We identified on average 24,700 methylated regions (MRs) per sample with a median length of 272 bp (mean: 856 bp).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative results from DMR analysis.

claim: For all three generations, DMRs mapped mainly to TEs and intergenic regions, and were three- to seven-fold over-represented in 2-kb regions upstream of transcription start sites compared with overall methylation in MRs.
source: For all three generations, DMRs mapped mainly to TEs and intergenic regions, and were three- to seven-fold over-represented in 2-kb regions upstream of transcription start sites compared with overall methylation in MRs (Figure 2A).
evidence: The manuscript presents genomic annotation analysis of DMRs.

claim: Methylation in CHG and CHH contexts at DMRs was significantly altered in stress-treated P0 versus control P0 samples.
source: However, methylation in CHG and CHH contexts at DMRs was significantly altered in stress-treated P0 versus control P0 samples (P < 0.01 in all generations, unpaired two-tailed Student's t-test) (Figure 2B; Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical test results showing significant methylation changes in specific contexts.

claim: For G3 and G5, the P1-descendants of salt-treated P0 plants formed a clear sub-group distinct from the control and P2 plants.
source: By contrast, for G3 and G5, the P1-descendants of salt-treated P0 plants formed a clear sub-group distinct from the control and P2 plants (Figure 2C).
evidence: The manuscript presents clustering analysis results showing distinct grouping patterns.

claim: The methylation patterns in P1-descendants correlate with the observed adaptive responses specifically in the P1, but not in the P2 progeny of G3 and G5 salt-treated plants.
source: These data concur with the adaptive responses we observed specifically in the P1, but not in the P2 progeny of G3 and G5 salt-treated plants (Figure 1C; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: The manuscript correlates methylation patterns with phenotypic observations.

claim: P2-descendants showed methylation patterns similar to control plants, which correlated with the observed lack of high salinity tolerance.
source: P2-descendants showed methylation patterns similar to control plants, which correlated with the observed lack of high salinity tolerance.
evidence: The manuscript correlates methylation patterns with phenotypic observations.

claim: Hyperosmotic stress directs DNA methylation changes primarily at non-CG sites located in intergenic TE-related sequences.
source: Thus, hyperosmotic stress directs DNA methylation changes primarily at non-CG sites located in intergenic TE-related sequences, and these epigenetic modifications are associated with an acquired transient adaptation to stress.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes findings about the genomic location and context of methylation changes.

claim: 49% of HS-DMRs in stressed plants (P0) overlapped with or were in close proximity (<500 bp) to DMRs that had been reported to arise spontaneously in mutation accumulation (MA) lines.
source: By contrast, 49% of HS-DMRs in stressed plants (P0) overlapped with or were in close proximity (<500 bp) to DMRs that had been reported to arise spontaneously in mutation accumulation (MA) lines that had been grown over 30 generations under controlled conditions (Figure 2D) (Becker et al., 2011; Hagmann et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript presents comparative analysis with published MA line data.

claim: Stress-triggered epigenetic reprogramming of specific genomic regions is not entirely random.
source: We compared pools of ten plants to identify HS-DMRs, while individual plants had been compared to define MA-DMRs. That there is nevertheless substantial overlap indicates that stress-triggered epigenetic reprogramming of specific genomic regions is not entirely random.
evidence: The manuscript infers from the overlap analysis that stress-induced methylation changes target specific regions.

claim: HS-DMRs that did not overlap with spontaneous MA-DMRs were enriched near genes with functions related to metabolic responses and ion transport.
source: In particular, HS-DMRs that did not overlap with spontaneous MA-DMRs were enriched near genes with functions related to metabolic responses and ion transport (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The manuscript presents gene ontology analysis results.

claim: Exposure to hyperosmotic stress targets discrete, epigenetically labile regions of the genome.
source: These data thus suggest that exposure to hyperosmotic stress targets discrete, epigenetically labile regions of the genome.
evidence: The manuscript draws conclusions from the DMR analysis about the nature of stress-induced methylation changes.

claim: Most HS-DMRs (81%) in G3 and G5 were hypermethylated in the hyperosmotic-treated P0 samples.
source: Most HS-DMRs (81%) in G3 and G5 were hypermethylated in the hyperosmotic-treated P0 samples, whereas G1 plants had similar number of hyper- and hypo-methylated DMRs (Figure 3A).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative analysis of methylation direction in DMRs.

claim: In progenies of stress-treated plants, the CHG and CHH methylation changes were gradually lost and reverted to the control states in the P1 and P2 progeny grown in the absence of stress.
source: Further, in progenies of stress-treated plants, the CHG and CHH methylation changes were gradually lost and reverted to the control states, as seen in the P1 and P2 progeny grown in the absence of stress (Figure 3A–B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing reversion of methylation changes over generations.

claim: Hyper-methylated HS-DMRs were significantly enriched near Helitrons.
source: Hyper-methylated HS-DMRs were significantly enriched near Helitrons (unpaired Student's t-test; **p<0.01) (Figure 3D), a TE family known to be targeted by RdDM (Nuthikattu et al., 2013), and near genes involved in RNA-directed DNA polymerase and reverse transcription activities (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The manuscript presents statistical analysis of TE family enrichment near DMRs.

claim: Hypo-methylated DMRs were found proximal to Copia, HAT, and Line L1 TEs.
source: In contrast, hypo-methylated DMRs were found proximal to Copia, HAT, and Line L1 TEs (Figure 3D).
evidence: The manuscript presents analysis of TE family distribution near DMRs.

claim: Copia, HAT, and Line L1 transposon families are targeted by DNA demethylases and are associated with gene expression response to environmental stress.
source: These transposon families are targeted by DNA demethylases and are associated with gene expression response to environmental stress (Le et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature to support the functional significance of specific TE families.

claim: drm1/drm2 plants did not show hyper-methylation in non-CG contexts after exposure to hyperosmotic stress.
source: To test whether RdDM was responsible for some of the HS-DMRs, we exposed drm1/drm2 double mutants to hyperosmotic stress over two consecutive generations. In contrast to wild-type, drm1/drm2 plants did not show hyper-methylation in non-CG contexts (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data from mutant analysis.

claim: No correlation was detected between methylation status and the presence of active siRNA production.
source: However, when we analysed public datasets for known siRNA loci (Fahlgren et al., 2010), we could not detect a correlation between methylation status and the presence of active siRNA production (Figure 3E).
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis of public siRNA data in relation to DMRs.

claim: HS-DMRs were enriched for hyperosmosis-altered tri-methylated lysine 27 in histone 3 (H3K27me3) compared to background MRs (63% vs. 13%).
source: Although hyperosmotic stress and growth conditions used by Sani et al., 2013 differed from ours, we found that HS-DMRs were enriched for hyperosmosis-altered tri-methylated lysine 27 in histone 3 (H3K27me3) compared to background MRs (63% vs. 13%) (Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents comparative analysis with published histone modification data.

claim: Hypermethylated HS-DMRs (38%) were associated with decreased H3K27me3, revealing an antagonistic relationship between these two repressive epigenetic marks.
source: Notably, hypermethylated HS-DMRs (38%) were associated with decreased H3K27me3, revealing an antagonistic relationship between these two repressive epigenetic marks in discrete genome regions involved in hyperosmotic priming.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the correlation between DNA methylation and histone modifications.

claim: Hyperosmotic stress induces transient DNA methylation and chromatin changes at intergenic elements derived from specific transposon families.
source: Collectively, our data show that hyperosmotic stress induces transient DNA methylation and chromatin changes at intergenic elements derived from specific transposon families.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes findings about the nature and location of stress-induced epigenetic changes.

claim: Enhanced tolerance to hyperosmotic stress conditions was primarily conferred through the female germline.
source: We found that enhanced tolerance to hyperosmotic stress conditions was primarily conferred through the female germline (Figure 4A).
evidence: The manuscript presents data from reciprocal crosses showing parent-of-origin effects.

claim: The progeny of dme-6 stressed plants were even more tolerant to hyperosmotic stress than that of stressed control plants.
source: We stressed dme-6 plants for two generations and tested the offspring for tolerance to hyperosmotic stress. The progeny of dme-6 stressed plants were even more tolerant to hyperosmotic stress (Student's t-test, p<0.001) than that of stressed control plants (Figure 4A), thus implicating DME's involvement in resetting stress-directed methylation marks in the male germline.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data from mutant analysis showing enhanced stress tolerance.

claim: DME is involved in resetting stress-directed methylation marks in the male germline.
source: The progeny of dme-6 stressed plants were even more tolerant to hyperosmotic stress (Student's t-test, p<0.001) than that of stressed control plants (Figure 4A), thus implicating DME's involvement in resetting stress-directed methylation marks in the male germline.
evidence: The manuscript infers from mutant phenotype data the role of DME in epigenetic resetting.

claim: DME diminishes the paternal transmission of hyperosmotic priming responses.
source: To confirm this hypothesis, we performed reciprocal crosses between unstressed wild-type and stressed heterozygous dme-6 plants (Figure 4A). The differential responses observed confirmed that DME diminishes the paternal transmission of hyperosmotic priming responses.
evidence: The manuscript presents data from reciprocal crosses confirming the role of DME.

claim: Hyperosmotic stress induced very few methylation changes in sperm cells (SC) and vegetative nuclei (VN).
source: Unlike in somatic tissue, hyperosmotic stress induced very few methylation changes in SC and VN (Figure 4B) such that only three DMRs became hypomethylated upon hyperosmotic treatment.
evidence: The manuscript presents methylome analysis of male gametes.

claim: 13,776 DMRs distinguished sperm cells from vegetative nuclei (SV-DMRs).
source: This strikingly contrasted with the13,776 DMRs that distinguished SCs from VNs (SV-DMRs) (Figure 4C).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative results from comparative methylome analysis.

claim: Over three quarters of the HS-DMRs (76%) overlapped with SV-DMRs.
source: Significantly, over three quarters of the HS-DMRs (76%) overlapped with SV-DMRs (Figure 4C) and half of them with MA-DMRs (Figure 2D).
evidence: The manuscript presents overlap analysis between different DMR sets.

claim: CHG methylation in sperm cells was elevated in pericentromeric regions, while methylation in vegetative nuclei was depleted in all sequence contexts and reduced to the central centromeric region.
source: Further, when compared with somatic tissues, CHG methylation in SC was elevated in pericentromeric regions, while methylation in VN was depleted in all sequence contexts and reduced to the central centromeric region (Figure 4E).
evidence: The manuscript presents genome-wide methylation patterns in male gametes.

claim: Most HS-DMRs were hyper-methylated in dme-6 sperm cells but hypo-methylated in dme-6 vegetative nuclei.
source: Most HS-DMRs were hyper-methylated in dme-6 sperm cells but hypo-methylated in dme-6 vegetative nuclei (Figure 4—figure supplemental 2).
evidence: The manuscript presents methylation analysis in dme mutant gametes.

claim: DNA glycosylase activity in the male germline is pivotal for both the epigenetic silencing of transposons and for the resetting of epigenetic marks induced by environmental stress.
source: In summary, DNA glycosylase activity in the male germline is pivotal for both the epigenetic silencing of transposons and for the resetting of epigenetic marks induced by environmental stress.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes findings about the role of DNA glycosylase in male gametes.

claim: Hyperosmotic priming effects are unequally transmitted through the male and female germlines.
source: As a consequence, the hyperosmotic priming effects are unequally transmitted through the male and female germlines.
evidence: The manuscript concludes from the data that there is parent-of-origin-dependent transmission of stress memory.

claim: 123 genes were flanked by HS-DMRs.
source: We found 123 genes that were flanked by HS-DMRs (Figure 2D) of which one third (32%) have been previously shown to be responsive to osmotic stress (Zeller et al., 2009) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 5).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative results from genomic annotation analysis.

claim: One third (32%) of genes flanked by HS-DMRs have been previously shown to be responsive to osmotic stress.
source: We found 123 genes that were flanked by HS-DMRs (Figure 2D) of which one third (32%) have been previously shown to be responsive to osmotic stress (Zeller et al., 2009) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 5).
evidence: The manuscript presents comparative analysis with published gene expression data.

claim: An HS-DMR upstream of MYB20 became hyper-methylated in P0 plants exposed to hyperosmotic stress, which was maintained in the P1 progeny of stressed plants, but then changed to levels similar to that seen in control plants in the P2 progeny.
source: We identified one HS-DMR overlapping two TEs (Figure 5A) that was found upstream of MYB DOMAIN PROTEIN 20 (MYB20), which encodes a transcription factor involved in abscisic acid (ABA) signalling and implicated in stress tolerance (Cui et al., 2013). This HS-DMR became hyper-methylated in P0 plants exposed to hyperosmotic stress, which was maintained in the P1 progeny of stressed plants, but then changed to levels similar to that seen in control plants in the P2 progeny.
evidence: The manuscript presents methylation analysis at a specific locus over multiple generations.

claim: MYB20 was strongly downregulated in P1 and P2 progeny when P0 plants had experienced hyperosmotic stress.
source: We did not detect MYB20 expression changes in response to high hyperosmotic treatment in plants whose progenitors had not experienced hyperosmotic stress (Figure 5B). However, when P0 plants had experienced such stress, this gene was strongly downregulated in P1 and P2 progeny (p-value 0.006) (Figure 5B).
evidence: The manuscript presents gene expression analysis showing transgenerational effects.

claim: The CNI1 HS-DMR had reduced DNA methylation in the P1 progeny of stressed plants, and remained hypomethylated in P2 progeny.
source: Another HS-DMR was located downstream of the CARBON/NITROGEN INSENSITIVE 1 (CNI1) gene (Figure 5A), which encodes a membrane RING-type ubiquitin ligase implicated in metabolic sensing (Sato et al., 2009). The CNI1 HS-DMR, which also overlapped a TE, had reduced DNA methylation in the P1 progeny of stressed plants, and remained hypomethylated in P2 progeny.
evidence: The manuscript presents methylation analysis at the CNI1 locus over multiple generations.

claim: Hyperosmotic stress strongly reduced CNI1 expression in progeny of untreated plants, and to a lesser extent in progeny of plants exposed to hyperosmotic stress.
source: Hyperosmotic stress strongly reduced CNI1 expression in progeny of untreated plants, and to a lesser extent in progeny of plants exposed to hyperosmotic stress (Figure 5C).
evidence: The manuscript presents gene expression analysis showing priming effects.

claim: The expression of MYB20, CNI1 and four other genes with associated HS-DMRs was altered in rdd demethylation mutants, independent of growth condition or priming.
source: Independent of growth condition or priming, the expression of MYB20, CNI1 and four other genes with associated HS-DMRs was altered in rdd demethylation mutants, and the transcriptional stress response in P1 progeny of stressed plants was impaired in RdDM mutants (Figure 5B–C; Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript presents gene expression analysis in epigenetic mutants.

claim: The transcriptional stress response in P1 progeny of stressed plants was impaired in RdDM mutants.
source: Independent of growth condition or priming, the expression of MYB20, CNI1 and four other genes with associated HS-DMRs was altered in rdd demethylation mutants, and the transcriptional stress response in P1 progeny of stressed plants was impaired in RdDM mutants (Figure 5B–C; Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript presents gene expression analysis in epigenetic mutants.

claim: Many genes encoding components of the DNA methylation and demethylation pathways were sensitive to hyperosmotic salt treatment.
source: We then assessed the transcriptional response of genes encoding components of the DNA methylation and demethylation pathways and found that many of them were sensitive to hyperosmotic salt treatment (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The manuscript presents gene expression analysis of epigenetic pathway genes.

claim: Methylation at regions corresponding to HS-DMRs was severely affected in met1 and rdd mutants.
source: Moreover, analysis of epigenomic data for RdDM and demethylation mutants (Stroud et al., 2013) revealed that methylation at regions corresponding to HS-DMRs from our data set was severely affected in met1 and rdd mutants (Fischer's Exact test p=0,005) (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The manuscript presents analysis of published epigenomic data for mutants.

claim: CNI1 sense transcription in both T-DNA insertion alleles was misregulated in response to stress.
source: We therefore analysed the effects of two independent mutant alleles, in which T-DNAs were inserted between the CNI1 transcription unit and the downstream HS-DMR, possibly impeding communication between the HS-DMR and the CNI1 locus (Figure 6A). As expected, CNI1 sense transcription in both insertion alleles was misregulated in response to stress (Figure 6B).
evidence: The manuscript presents gene expression analysis in insertion mutants.

claim: Deletion of the HS-DMR sequence reduced downregulation of sense CNI1 transcripts in response to hyperosmotic stress.
source: To demonstrate the functional relevance of the sequence targeted epigenetically after hyperosmotic-stress, we generated a deletion line (Δcni1-DMR) using CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing (Jinek et al., 2012) (Figure 6A; Figure 6—figure supplement 1). Deletion of the HS-DMR sequence reduced downregulation of sense CNI1 transcripts in response to hyperosmotic stress (Figure 6C), indicating that this HS-DMR acts as a distant regulatory element.
evidence: The manuscript presents gene expression analysis in CRISPR deletion mutants.

claim: The CNI1 HS-DMR acts as a distant regulatory element.
source: Deletion of the HS-DMR sequence reduced downregulation of sense CNI1 transcripts in response to hyperosmotic stress (Figure 6C), indicating that this HS-DMR acts as a distant regulatory element.
evidence: The manuscript infers from deletion mutant data the regulatory function of the HS-DMR.

claim: Methylation in IR hairpin transgenic lines remained even under hyperosmotic stress.
source: Finally, to demonstrate directly that the methylation status of this element determines its activity, we introduced an inverted repeat (IR) hairpin (Matzke et al., 2002) that directs DNA methylation to the CNI1 HS-DMR by RdDM (Figure 6A). McrBC assays and bisulfite sequencing confirmed that methylation in IR hairpin transgenic lines remained even under hyperosmotic stress (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript presents methylation analysis in transgenic lines.

claim: Levels of CNI1 sense transcript in response to stress were no longer reduced in IR hairpin transgenic plants.
source: Levels of CNI1 sense transcript in response to stress were no longer reduced in these plants (Figure 6D), thus strengthening the argument that the CNI1 HS-DMR acts as an epigenetically sensitive regulatory element.
evidence: The manuscript presents gene expression analysis in transgenic lines.

claim: The CNI1 HS-DMR acts as an epigenetically sensitive regulatory element.
source: Levels of CNI1 sense transcript in response to stress were no longer reduced in these plants (Figure 6D), thus strengthening the argument that the CNI1 HS-DMR acts as an epigenetically sensitive regulatory element.
evidence: The manuscript concludes from transgenic and mutant data the regulatory function of the HS-DMR.

claim: Hyperosmotic stress increased expression of a lncRNA (CNI1-AS1) that is transcribed in the antisense direction and overlaps with CNI1 in control plants.
source: We found that hyperosmotic stress increased expression of a lncRNA that is transcribed in the antisense direction and overlaps with CNI1, both in control plants (CNI1-AS1) (Figure 6—figure supplement 3) and in the progeny of plants that had gone through our control non-salt conditions (p-value 0.004; Figure 6E).
evidence: The manuscript presents lncRNA expression analysis.

claim: Hyperosmotic stress reduced expression of CNI1-AS1 lncRNA in progeny of plants exposed to hyperosmotic stress.
source: By contrast, hyperosmotic stress reduced expression of this lncRNA in progeny of plants exposed to hyperosmotic stress (p-value 0.015; Figure 6E).
evidence: The manuscript presents lncRNA expression analysis showing priming effects.

claim: The hyperosmotic responsiveness of CNI1-AS1 was impaired in progeny of rdd mutants.
source: That this was linked to differential methylation was indicated by the hyperosmotic responsiveness of CNI1-AS1 being impaired in progeny of rdd mutants (Figure 6E).
evidence: The manuscript presents lncRNA expression analysis in mutants.

claim: In the two insertion alleles and in the deletion line, the stress-mediated transcriptional response of CNI1-AS1 was altered.
source: In the two insertion alleles and in the deletion line, the stress-mediated transcriptional response was similarly altered (Figure 6F).
evidence: The manuscript presents lncRNA expression analysis in mutants.

claim: The HS-DMR downstream of CNI1 acts as an epigenetic sensor that controls CNI1 expression by modulating the expression of an antisense lncRNA.
source: These data support a model in which the HS-DMR downstream of CNI1 acts as an epigenetic sensor that controls CNI1 expression by modulating the expression of an antisense lncRNA.
evidence: The manuscript proposes a mechanistic model based on the experimental data.

claim: lncRNA expression was insensitive to hyperosmotic stress in IR hairpin lines.
source: Our finding that lncRNA expression was insensitive to hyperosmotic stress in IR hairpin lines (Figure 6G) adds further weight to this model.
evidence: The manuscript presents lncRNA expression analysis in transgenic lines supporting the proposed model.

claim: Only stress-responsive genes adjacent to HS-DMRs (not MA-DMRs) were enriched for hyperosmotic-responsive antisense lncRNAs.
source: To investigate whether there might be a broader role for lncRNAs in mediating the effects of stress induced DMRs, we comparatively analysed all stress-responsive genes adjacent to HS-DMRs and to MA-DMRs. Only the first group was enriched for hyperosmotic-responsive antisense lncRNAs (Fisher's Exact test, p=0.008) (Supplementary file 6), indicating that HS-DMRs preferentially act as regulatory elements of stress-induced antisense lncRNAs.
evidence: The manuscript presents statistical analysis comparing HS-DMRs and MA-DMRs.

claim: HS-DMRs preferentially act as regulatory elements of stress-induced antisense lncRNAs.
source: Only the first group was enriched for hyperosmotic-responsive antisense lncRNAs (Fisher's Exact test, p=0.008) (Supplementary file 6), indicating that HS-DMRs preferentially act as regulatory elements of stress-induced antisense lncRNAs.
evidence: The manuscript infers from enrichment analysis the regulatory role of HS-DMRs.

claim: Intergenerational priming responses to hyperosmotic stress are triggered by recurrent exposure to stimuli, but this response is rapidly lost in the absence of stress.
source: Our main conclusion is that intergenerational priming responses to hyperosmotic stress are triggered by recurrent exposure to stimuli, but that this response is rapidly lost in the absence of stress.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the main conclusion from the study.

claim: Hyperosmotic stress directs DNA methylation changes primarily to discrete genome regions that are rich in TE-related sequences.
source: Bycontrast, using our highly controlled and replicated syste, and a strict method for detecting methylated regions, we found no clear evidence for such indiscriminate changes. Instead, we found that hyperosmotic stress directs DNA methylation changes primarily to discrete genome regions that are rich in TE-related sequences (Figures 2 and 3).
evidence: The manuscript contrasts their findings with previous reports and summarizes their observations.

claim: The dynamic DNA methylation changes are of functional consequence because the adaptive response is impaired in mutants defective in DNA methylation pathways.
source: The dynamic DNA methylation changes are of functional consequence because the adaptive response is impaired in mutants defective in DNA methylation pathways (Figure 1), which are also known to regulate TE activity (Kim and Zilberman, 2014).
evidence: The manuscript infers functional significance from mutant phenotype data.

claim: A small fraction of acquired epigenetic changes is transmitted to the immediate offspring only after recurrent stress exposure, but in the absence of a renewed stimulus these are reset in subsequent generations.
source: A small fraction of acquired epigenetic changes is transmitted to the immediate offspring only after recurrent stress exposure, but in the absence of a renewed stimulus these are reset in subsequent generations.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes findings about the transgenerational dynamics of epigenetic changes.

claim: Epigenetic stress memory in annual plant species may be transient in nature.
source: This implies that epigenetic stress memory in annual plant species may be transient in nature, however this response may differ in perennial plants that grow over longer periods of time before producing any offspring or in plants that reproduce asexually.
evidence: The manuscript speculates about the broader implications of their findings.

claim: Half of the newly acquired methylation changes identified in stressed plants overlapped with regions privileged for epimutation also found in near-isogenic greenhouse-grown populations.
source: Half of the newly acquired methylation changes identified in our stressed plants overlapped with regions privileged for epimutation also found in near-isogenic greenhouse-grown populations (Figure 2) (Hagmann et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript presents comparative analysis with published MA line data.

claim: Distinct regions of the plant epigenome are particularly labile, and such acquired epimutations could modulate the ability of plants to respond to stress.
source: This finding confirms that distinct regions of the plant epigenome are particularly labile, and it suggests that such acquired epimutations could modulate the ability of plants to respond to stress.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the overlap with MA-DMRs to support the concept of epigenetically labile regions.

claim: Enhanced stress responses were only passed on after two consecutive generations of stress exposure, but not when plants were exposed to hyperosmotic stress for only one episode.
source: Importantly, in our system, enhanced stress responses were only passed on after two consecutive generations of stress exposure, but not when plants were exposed to hyperosmotic stress for only one episode, which may be the reason why previous studies often failed to find clear evidence for inheritance of stress-induced epigenetic changes (Eichten and Springer, 2015; Secco et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript explains their findings in the context of previous studies.

claim: Repeated stress exposure being required for induction of transiently heritable stress resistance may reside in the importance of poised epigenetic states for environmental priming.
source: One explanation for repeated stress exposure being required for induction of transiently heritable stress resistance may reside in the importance of poised epigenetic states for environmental priming (Jaskiewicz et al., 2011; Sani et al., 2013), which in turn may facilitate the establishment of new epigenetic marks at discrete genomic regions that are sensitive to stress.
evidence: The manuscript proposes a mechanistic explanation based on published concepts.

claim: There is substantial overlap (>30%) between HS-DMRs established in recurrently stressed generations and dynamic chromatin occupancy directed by hyperosmosis.
source: This view is supported by the substantial overlap (>30%) between HS-DMRs established in recurrently stressed generations (Figure 2) and dynamic chromatin occupancy directed by hyperosmosis (Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents overlap analysis supporting their mechanistic explanation.

claim: Recurrent exposure to hyperosmotic stress did not significantly increase the number of newly acquired epimutations.
source: Intriguingly, recurrent exposure to hyperosmotic stress did not significantly increase the number of newly acquired epimutations, suggesting that the extent of epigenetic plasticity elicited by the environment is limited to a few key genomic regions that may be under purifying selection (Hollister and Gaut, 2009).
evidence: The manuscript reports observations about the number of epimutations across generations.

claim: The extent of epigenetic plasticity elicited by the environment is limited to a few key genomic regions that may be under purifying selection.
source: Intriguingly, recurrent exposure to hyperosmotic stress did not significantly increase the number of newly acquired epimutations, suggesting that the extent of epigenetic plasticity elicited by the environment is limited to a few key genomic regions that may be under purifying selection (Hollister and Gaut, 2009).
evidence: The manuscript infers evolutionary implications from the observation about limited epigenetic plasticity.

claim: Certain genomic regions are epigenetically targeted, depending on the type of stress because the DNA methylation changes induced by hyperosmotic stress did not overlap with methylation changes reported for other abiotic stresses.
source: It is likely that certain genomic regions are epigenetically targeted, depending on the type of stress because the DNA methylation changes induced by hyperosmotic stress did not overlap with methylation changes reported for other abiotic stresses (Seymour et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript infers stress-specificity from lack of overlap with other stress studies.

claim: Hyperosmotic priming responses were transmitted primarily through the maternal germline.
source: Our analyses revealed that hyperosmotic priming responses were transmitted primarily through the maternal germline (Figure 4).
evidence: The manuscript summarizes findings from reciprocal cross experiments.

claim: Most of the stress-associated methylation changes in leaves were largely absent in mature male gametes.
source: We attribute this difference to differences in the meiotic transmission of newly acquired DNA methylation marks. In support of this hypothesis, most of the stress-associated methylation changes in leaves were largely absent in mature male gametes (Figure 4), indicating that environmentally directed epigenetic marks are more efficiently reset in male rather than in female gametes.
evidence: The manuscript presents methylome data from male gametes supporting parent-of-origin effects.

claim: Environmentally directed epigenetic marks are more efficiently reset in male rather than in female gametes.
source: In support of this hypothesis, most of the stress-associated methylation changes in leaves were largely absent in mature male gametes (Figure 4), indicating that environmentally directed epigenetic marks are more efficiently reset in male rather than in female gametes.
evidence: The manuscript infers differential resetting between male and female gametes from methylome data.

claim: Male gametes undergo an active reprogramming of DNA methylation at transposon sequences by the DNA glycosylase DME.
source: Indeed, not only do male gametes undergo an active reprogramming of DNA methylation at transposon sequences by the DNA glycosylase DME (Borges et al., 2012a; Ibarra et al., 2012), but also at stress-dependent DNA methylation sites (Figure 4).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature and presents their own data about DME function.

claim: The enhanced tolerance to hyperosmotic stress in progeny of stressed dme-6 plants implicates DNA demethylation both in the active reprogramming of TEs and in the resetting of environmentally-directed epigenetic changes in male gametes.
source: Moreover, the enhanced tolerance to hyperosmotic stress in progeny of stressed dme-6 plants implicates DNA demethylation both in the active reprogramming of TEs and in the resetting of environmentally-directed epigenetic changes in male gametes.
evidence: The manuscript infers dual roles of DME from mutant phenotype data.

claim: Female gametes reside on the mother plant where they are eventually fertilised by sperm from pollen that may have travelled a great distance from its male progenitor to produce seed.
source: One explanation is that female gametes reside on the mother plant where they are eventually fertilised by sperm from pollen that may have travelled a great distance from its male progenitor to produce seed.
evidence: The manuscript draws on general biological knowledge about plant reproduction.

claim: Given that seed dispersal usually occurs at a short distance from the mother, a solely maternal transmission of the newly acquired epigenetic marks would be an efficient way of retaining only the most relevant parental stress-associated adaptive responses in the progeny.
source: Given that seed dispersal usually occurs at a short distance from the mother, a solely maternal transmission of the newly acquired epigenetic marks would be an efficient way of retaining only the most relevant parental stress-associated adaptive responses in the progeny.
evidence: The manuscript proposes an evolutionary explanation for maternal transmission based on ecological reasoning.

claim: Environmentally-induced priming responses involve DNA (de)methylation pathways that control the extent to which acquired epigenetic states are inherited and maintained in successive generations.
source: Our study has revealed that environmentally-induced priming responses involve DNA (de)methylation pathways that control the extent to which acquired epigenetic states are inherited and maintained in successive generations (Figure 1).
evidence: The manuscript summarizes findings about the role of DNA methylation pathways.

claim: Stress can specifically alter methylation at the adjacent sequences of several key stress-response regulators.
source: We now provide compelling evidence that stress can specifically alter methylation at the adjacent sequences of several key stress-response regulators (Figures 2, 5 and 6), a process that is mediated by the RdDM and DNA demethylation pathways (Figure 7).
evidence: The manuscript summarizes findings about targeted methylation changes at regulatory genes.

claim: Some TEs proximal to upstream regions and sensitive to methylation changes directed by hyperosmotic stress have regulatory roles.
source: Targeted studies have revealed that some TEs proximal to upstream regions and sensitive to methylation changes directed by hyperosmotic stress have regulatory roles (Baek et al., 2011; Xu et al., 2015) and are associated with quantitative traits and adaptive behaviour (Baxter et al., 2012; Busoms et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature about regulatory roles of TEs.

claim: Both DNA methylation and demethylation activities are tightly regulated by the action of adjacent upstream TEs that act as an epigenetic sensors.
source: Notably, both DNA methylation and demethylation activities are also tightly regulated by the action of adjacent upstream TEs that act as an epigenetic sensors (Lei et al., 2015; Williams et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature about TE-mediated regulation of epigenetic pathways.

claim: HS-DMRs are preferentially associated with the transcription of antisense lncRNAs.
source: The epigenetic regulation of HS-DMRs is not always associated with upstream regulatory sequences and sense transcription; instead we found that they are preferentially associated with the transcription of antisense lncRNAs (Figure 6).
evidence: The manuscript summarizes findings about the association between HS-DMRs and lncRNAs.

claim: Antisense lncRNAs have been implicated in directing chromatin changes.
source: Although the functions of these HS-DMR-associated non-coding transcripts are largely unknown, antisense lncRNAs have been implicated in directing chromatin changes (Ariel et al., 2014; Heo and Sung, 2011; Swiezewski et al., 2009), and thereby in influencing transcription, splicing and transcript stability (Bardou et al., 2014; Borsani et al., 2005).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature about lncRNA functions.

claim: Antisense lncRNAs were shown to be regulated by epigenetically labile control elements sensitive to stress.
source: In this study,antisense lncRNAs were shown to be regulated by epigenetically labile control elements sensitive to stress (Figure 7).
evidence: The manuscript summarizes their findings about lncRNA regulation.

claim: Methylation changes in HS-DMR genome regions could modulate transcription factor binding or chromatin regulatory loops.
source: Methylation changes in these genome regions could modulate transcription factor binding (Zhong et al., 2013) or chromatin regulatory loops (Ariel et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript speculates about mechanisms based on published literature.

claim: The adaptive value of epigenetic inheritance over multiple generations must depend on the cost of epigenetic resetting, as well as on the degree and predictability of environmental stress.
source: The adaptive value of this inheritance over multiple generations must depend on the cost of epigenetic resetting, as well as on the degree and predictability of environmental stress (Herman et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript discusses evolutionary considerations based on published theoretical work.

claim: An adaptive bet-hedging strategy that is mediated by increased epigenetic variation could be advantageous in highly stochastic natural environments.
source: Because conditions in many natural environments are highly stochastic, an adaptive bet-hedging strategy (Simons, 2011) that is mediated by increased epigenetic variation could be advantageous.
evidence: The manuscript discusses evolutionary implications based on published theory.

claim: Under controlled stress conditions, the contribution of adaptive epigenetic variation shows parental effects, which may be favoured over bet-hedging in relatively stable environments.
source: Under our controlled stress conditions, the contribution of adaptive epigenetic variation shows parental effects (Figure 4), which may be favoured over bet-hedging in relatively stable environments (Kuijper and Johnstone, 2016).
evidence: The manuscript discusses evolutionary implications of their findings based on published theory.
